paper.title: Notes on Catalytic P Systems
paper.abstract: In this paper we address the possibility of studying the computational capabilities of catalytic P systems with one catalyst by the means of iterated finite state transducers (IFT). In particular, we focus on a variant of catalytic P systems which satisfies in addition to the original definition the following property: if in a region of the P system an object is the subject of a catalytic rule, then in the same region it must exists also a non-cooperative rule that rewrites the same object. Finally, we also give a normal form for catalytic P systems.

verdict.summary: Short theoretical note in membrane computing: a normal-form theorem for catalytic P systems and an inclusion of mixed one-catalyst P systems in length sets of 3-state iterated finite transducers. Formalism is native to the subject and proportionate; proofs are sketched rather than fully rigorous.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Computational power of catalytic P systems with one catalyst, studied by simulating a restricted ("mixed") variant with iterated finite state transducers (IFTs); plus a Chomsky-like normal form for catalytic P systems.
**Level:** 4 (High)
**Rationale:** The paper proves language-family inclusion results in formal language / computability theory (N OP1(Mcat1) ⊆ N IFT3) and a normal-form equivalence. This is computability-theoretic work, above Level 3. It does not itself prove universality or undecidability, so Level 5 was not assigned (defaulting lower).

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 3 (IFT as a tuple, catalytic P system as a construct, mixed P system restriction; configuration/computation semantics given inline)
- Theorems: 3 (Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Corollary 3)
- Proofs: 2
- Equations: numerous rule schemes and set constructions (O', R1', sets X, Y, T, K, V, F)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 3×2 + 3×3 + 2×4 = 23
Expected range (Level 4): 30-80
Ratio: 0.29x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The tuple definitions and set notation are the native language of formal language theory and are required to state and prove the inclusion results; the Necessity Test passes for each element because the results cannot be stated or argued without them.

### Issues
- The proof of Theorem 1 constructs only the rules simulating non-cooperative rules and says the catalytic case is "defined similarly, therefore we will not present them here"; the proof is therefore incomplete as written.
- The proof of Theorem 1 contains an unresolved cross-reference ("As we already stated in Section ??").
- The proof of Theorem 2 is an informal argument about the IFT construction; the claimed bijective correspondence between configurations and strings is asserted rather than shown in detail. The text also refers to states "qi ... 1 ≤ i ≤ 3" while the states are q0, q1, q2.
- These are quality-of-proof concerns, not formalism theater.

---

## Citation Analysis

One self-citation out of seven references (14.3%): [7] Sburlan, P systems with promoters/inhibitors, cited for the known result that the number of membranes can be reduced to one. It is directly relevant (same field, used in the argument). References [4] and [5] (Păun monograph and handbook) are listed but not cited in the text. No concerning patterns.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are formal statements supported by (sketched) proofs; background results are attributed to [1], [2], [7]. The paper acknowledges open problems inline: Remark 4.1 states conjectures and notes "It remains an open problem whether or not this restriction is important for the overall simulation", which counts as inline acknowledgement of limitations. Figures 1 and 2 are not available in the text extraction. No artifacts are relevant to a pure theory paper; none are offered. No instructions addressed to reviewers or automated assessors were found in the text.

---

## Conclusion

A compact theoretical note whose formal apparatus is proportionate and necessary for its subject. Its main weaknesses are the completeness and rigour of the proofs (an omitted case in Theorem 1, a broken section reference, an informal simulation argument in Theorem 2) and its modest scope: the main result is an inclusion that converts an open problem rather than resolving it. No integrity flags apply.
